title: Contrasting patterns of divergence and gene flow in subspecies of a forest-dwelling harvestman Leiobunum japanense (Eupnoi: Opiliones: Arachnida)
content:
Abstract
The complex geological and climatic history of Japan has shaped its rich biodiversity, making it an ideal setting in which to study the dispersal and diversification of endemic species. Leiobunum japanense has been divided into two subspecies based on morphological traits. However, the genetic structure and evolutionary history of these subspecies remain poorly understood. In this study, we analysed mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) sequences and single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) to investigate the genetic diversity, dispersal history, and subspecies’ delineations of L. japanense. We identified three distinct lineages: the eastern, western, and Kyushu lineages. The eastern and western lineages correspond to the two subspecies based on morphology, whereas the Kyushu lineage may represent a cryptic species, as it is morphologically similar to, but genetically distinct from, the western lineage. Divergence time estimates suggest that the Kyushu lineage split approximately 3.8 million years ago (Mya), and the eastern and western lineages diverged around 2.8 Mya. Our findings also highlight an intriguing discrepancy in fixation indices between the mtDNA and SNP results in the western lineages, with mtDNA haplotypes showing broad geographic distributions, whereas SNPs revealed fine-scale genetic differentiation. This finding suggests a female-biased dispersal pattern, potentially influenced by behavioural or ecological traits.
